soundcheck.heard: What would make an AI-fishing rule worth testing? A September 11th paper explores that question with Eastern Bering Sea Pollock. Researchers affiliated with the Alaska Fisheries Science Center built simulations informed by historical observations. Their agent practices harvest choices through repeated simulated seasons. Feedback rewards outcomes and changes the learned rule. They compare it with a predefined harvest rule. Will an advantage hold when the biology changes? Start with a model where young fish enter at a constant rate. The learned policy leaves more spawning biomass, the weight of breeding fish than its comparison. Alongside large annual catch swings. The next experiment links young fish entering the stock to the breeding population. This is a separate simulated case with its own comparison. Here, the learned rule catches more and leaves less breeding biomass than that comparison. These simulated gains may offer no management advantage over a predefined rule. In real fisheries, no fisheries and the North Pacific Fishery Management Council manage Alaska Pollock. Fishing businesses need sound management to plan their seasons. So test both rules against the same catch pattern and breeding stock goals. These are illustrative simulations with public code. They establish alternatives to investigate, not a winning real world policy. Which balance should a rule demonstrate between catches and breeding fish?
